title: Teaching
text:
My teaching combines substantive sociology with empirical research practice. I aim to help students develop a strong understanding of sociological theories and social structures while also learning how to formulate research questions, work with data, evaluate evidence, and draw well-founded conclusions.
I see theoretical reasoning and data analysis as part of the same sociological process. Quantitative methods are therefore not taught as ends in themselves, but as tools for investigating substantive questions about inequality, social structure, migration, trust, and social change.

title: Scott Milligan
text:
I’m an applied sociologist and quantitative social scientist interested in how social inequalities shape people’s life chances and the societies they live in. My work combines substantive sociological questions with empirical analysis, particularly around social inequality, migration, diversity, trust, and social cohesion.
I work mainly with quantitative and internationally comparative data, including survey and longitudinal data, to examine how inequalities emerge, persist, and vary across institutional and national contexts. More recently, my work has expanded into child and youth wellbeing, health inequalities, disability, and institutional access: when do institutions reproduce existing disadvantages, and when can they help to offset them?
I also have a strong interest in open science, reproducible research, data harmonisation, and research infrastructure. These interests shape how I approach empirical work, with an emphasis on transparent and well-documented workflows that make data and analytical decisions easier to understand, verify, and reuse.
In recent years, my work has increasingly combined research with research coordination and project development, particularly in international and interdisciplinary settings.

title: Research
text: My research focuses on social inequality and social structure, particularly on the ways in which inequalities shape individual life chances, social participation, and broader social relationships. I am especially interested in how these processes vary across institutional and national contexts. I am also committed to open science and reproducible research, with a particular interest in transparent, well-documented workflows that make data, analytical decisions, and research outputs easier to understand, verify, and reuse.

title: Research
section: Social inequality, migration, and social cohesion
text:
Social inequality, migration, and social cohesion
A longstanding strand of my research examines the relationship between social inequality, migration-related diversity, trust, tolerance, and social cohesion.
Using international comparative survey data and multilevel approaches, I have studied how economic inequality and poverty relate to tolerance, how immigration and ethnicity shape civic participation, and how social and national contexts influence trust and cohesion.
A central question in this work is why similar levels of inequality or diversity can have very different social consequences across societies.

title: Research
text:
Inequality, institutional access, and participation
My more recent work extends these interests to health, wellbeing, disability, and institutional access.
I am interested in the conditions under which institutions reproduce or mitigate existing inequalities. This includes questions about access to education, healthcare, support services, and labour-market opportunities, and about how individual social position interacts with institutional structures.
Current project development includes research on social inequalities among people with disabilities and on health literacy and healthcare utilisation.

title: Research
text:
International comparative quantitative research
My research is primarily quantitative and internationally comparative. I work with survey and longitudinal data and use approaches including multilevel and panel analysis to connect individual experiences and outcomes with institutional and societal contexts.
